# Probability of 50 Trillion or More Successes

## Setting Up the Problem

We have a binomial random variable:
- $n = 100 \text{ trillion} = 10^{14}$ (number of trials)
- $p = 0.1$ (success probability)
- We want $P(X \geq 50 \text{ trillion}) = P(X \geq 5 \times 10^{13})$

## Computing the Mean and Standard Deviation

$$\mu = np = 10^{14} \times 0.1 = 10^{13} = 10 \text{ trillion}$$

$$\sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{10^{14} \times 0.1 \times 0.9} = \sqrt{9 \times 10^{12}} = 3 \times 10^6 = 3 \text{ million}$$

## Computing the Z-Score

$$z = \frac{50 \times 10^{12} - 10 \times 10^{12}}{3 \times 10^6} = \frac{40 \times 10^{12}}{3 \times 10^6} = \frac{40}{3} \times 10^6 \approx 13{,}333{,}333$$

## Evaluating the Tail Probability

The z-score of approximately **13.3 million** standard deviations above the mean is extraordinarily extreme. The normal tail probability at this distance is on the order of:

$$P(Z \geq 13{,}333{,}333) \sim e^{-z^2/2} \sim e^{-8.89 \times 10^{13}}$$

This number is so fantastically small (with over 38 million zeros after the decimal point before the first non-zero digit) that the probability is **indistinguishable from zero** in any physical or practical sense.

## Conclusion

Obtaining 50 trillion or more successes when the expected number is only 10 trillion (a deviation of over 13 million standard deviations) has a probability that is:

$$\boxed{0}$$
